learn: Fluent readers read accurately, at a good pace and with expression, so their reading sounds like talking.
Fluency matters because when you don't have to work hard on every word, your brain can focus on meaning.
Rereading a passage several times, and reading aloud with a partner, are proven ways to build fluency.
check: What are the three parts of fluency?
Your brain can focus on meaning
lessons.try: Read the same paragraph aloud three times. Notice how it gets smoother each time.

learn: Strong readers notice when they stop understanding. This is called monitoring.
When something is confusing, you can reread, read ahead, look at pictures, or use context clues.
Stopping to ask "What just happened?" every page or two keeps you on track.
check: What can you do when confused?
Which question keeps you on track?
lessons.try: While reading, stop after each page and retell what happened in one sentence.

learn: A reading log records the title, pages read and a short thought about each book.
Setting goals, like finishing one chapter book each week, builds reading habits.
Trying different genres, such as mystery, biography, fantasy and poetry, makes you a well-rounded reader.
check: What does a reading log record?
Title, pages and a short thought
lessons.try: Start a reading log and set a goal for this month.

learn: A prefix is a word part added to the beginning of a word that changes its meaning.
un- means not: unhappy. re- means again: reread. pre- means before: preview. dis- means opposite: disagree.
Knowing prefixes helps you figure out new words.
lessons.try: Add un-, re- or dis- to five words and write what each new word means.

learn: A suffix is added to the end of a word.
-ful means full of: hopeful. -less means without: fearless. -er can mean a person who: teacher. -ly often means in a way: slowly.
Sometimes spelling changes: happy becomes happily.
lessons.try: Find five words with suffixes in a book you're reading.

learn: Context clues are hints in the nearby words that help you understand a new word.
"The enormous elephant was so big it couldn't fit through the gate." The clue "so big" tells you enormous means very large.
A dictionary lists words in alphabetical order with their meanings and pronunciations.
lessons.try: Find a new word in a book, guess its meaning from context, then check a dictionary.

learn: A character trait describes what a character is like inside: brave, honest, selfish, curious.
Traits are shown by actions and words. If a character returns a lost wallet, that shows honesty.
Always give evidence from the text for the traits you name.
check: What a character is like inside
What should you give for a trait?
lessons.try: Name two traits for a character in your book and give evidence for each.

learn: Motivation is why a character does something.
A character may act out of love, fear, jealousy or a wish to be accepted.
Understanding motivation helps you predict what the character will do next.
lessons.try: Explain why a character in your book made an important choice.

learn: A character's choices drive the plot forward.
In "The Boy Who Cried Wolf", the boy chooses to trick the villagers. When a real wolf comes, no one believes him.
Ask: what would have happened if the character chose differently?
check: Why didn't the villagers believe the boy?
Thinking about different choices helps you...
lessons.try: Rewrite the ending of a fable by changing one character's choice.

learn: A fable is a short tale, usually with animal characters, that teaches a moral.
Aesop was a storyteller in ancient Greece. His fables include "The Fox and the Grapes" and "The Lion and the Mouse".
In "The Lion and the Mouse", a tiny mouse frees a lion from a net. The moral: even small friends can be a big help.
lessons.try: Read "The Lion and the Mouse" and write its moral in your own words.

learn: Folktales are stories passed down by people telling them aloud for generations.
Many cultures have similar folktales. Cinderella stories exist in China (Yeh-Shen), Egypt (Rhodopis) and France.
Folktales often show a culture's values, like kindness or cleverness.
check: Yeh-Shen is a Cinderella story from...
lessons.try: Compare two Cinderella stories from different countries.

learn: A myth is a traditional story that explains something in nature or tells about gods and heroes.
The ancient Greeks told of Persephone, whose time below the earth each year explained winter.
Norse myths tell of Thor, whose hammer was said to make thunder.
check: What does a myth often explain?
In Norse myths, Thor's hammer made...
lessons.try: Write your own short myth explaining why the sky is blue.

learn: The main idea is the most important point the author wants you to understand.
Sometimes it's stated in a topic sentence. Sometimes you have to figure it out from the details.
Ask: what is this mostly about?
check: Where is the main idea sometimes stated?
lessons.try: Read a nonfiction article and write its main idea in one sentence.

learn: Key details are facts, examples or reasons that support the main idea.
If the main idea is "Bats are helpful animals", details might be "Bats eat insects" and "Bats pollinate plants".
Not every detail is key. Some are interesting but don't support the main idea.
lessons.try: List three key details that support your main idea.

learn: A summary is a short retelling of the main idea and key details in your own words.
Leave out small details and opinions.
A good summary is much shorter than the original.
check: A short retelling in your own words
A copy of the whole text
What should a summary leave out?
lessons.try: Write a three-sentence summary of a short article.

learn: Text features help readers find and understand information.
Headings, subheadings, bold words, captions, maps, diagrams, timelines and sidebars are all text features.
A sidebar is a box with extra information next to the main text.
lessons.try: Find five different text features in a nonfiction book.

learn: Authors organise information in structures.
Sequence tells steps in order. Compare and contrast shows how things are alike and different. Cause and effect explains why something happens.
Problem and solution describes a problem and how it was solved.
check: Which structure tells steps in order?
Which structure shows how things are alike and different?
lessons.try: Read a short article and name its structure.

learn: Signal words help you spot the structure.
First, next, finally signal sequence. Because, so, as a result signal cause and effect.
Both, however, unlike signal compare and contrast.
lessons.try: Underline signal words in a paragraph.

learn: Pronouns replace nouns: he, she, it, they, we.
Subjects and verbs must agree: "The dog runs." "The dogs run."
Pronouns must match their nouns: "Maria lost her hat."
lessons.try: Rewrite a paragraph using pronouns to avoid repeating names.

learn: Comparatives compare two things: taller, faster, more careful.
Superlatives compare three or more: tallest, fastest, most careful.
Some are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst.
check: The ___ of the three runners won.
lessons.try: Compare three animals using -er and -est words.

learn: Use commas in a list: "I packed socks, shoes, and a hat."
Use commas in addresses: Austin, Texas.
Quotation marks go around exact words someone says: "Let's go," said Ana.
check: Where do commas go in a list?
What goes around someone's exact words?
lessons.try: Write a short conversation between two characters with correct punctuation.

learn: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea.
The topic sentence tells the main idea of the paragraph, often at the start.
A strong topic sentence makes readers want to keep reading.
check: What does a topic sentence tell?
lessons.try: Write three different topic sentences about your favourite animal.

learn: Supporting sentences give facts, examples and details about the topic.
Most paragraphs have three to five supporting sentences.
Every sentence should connect to the topic.
check: Should every sentence connect to the topic?
Most paragraphs have about how many supporting sentences?
lessons.try: Write a paragraph with a topic sentence and three supporting sentences.

learn: Transitions connect ideas: also, for example, in addition, another reason.
A closing sentence wraps up the paragraph.
The closing often restates the main idea in new words.
check: What does a closing sentence do?
lessons.try: Add transitions and a closing sentence to your paragraph.

learn: A good narrative has characters, a setting, a problem, events and a resolution.
Plan with a story mountain: beginning, rising action, climax, falling action, ending.
The climax is the most exciting point, where the problem is faced.
lessons.try: Draw a story mountain for a story you want to write.

learn: Instead of telling "Sam was scared," show it: "Sam's knees shook and his voice came out as a whisper."
Use the senses: what do characters see, hear, smell, taste and feel?
Dialogue and action bring characters to life.
check: Which shows that Sam was scared?
lessons.try: Rewrite "It was a hot day" by showing, not telling.

learn: A strong ending solves the problem and shows how the character feels or changed.
Revise by reading aloud and asking: Is it clear? Is it exciting? Does it make sense?
Edit for spelling, capitals and punctuation last.
lessons.try: Revise your story, then ask someone to read it and give one suggestion.

learn: An opinion essay states a clear opinion, gives reasons with examples, and ends with a conclusion.
Linking words like because, therefore, since and for example connect opinions and reasons.
Strong reasons are supported by facts, not just feelings.
lessons.try: Write an opinion essay: Should students have homework?

learn: Research starts with a question: How do bees make honey?
Use several sources: books, encyclopaedias and trusted websites ending in .gov or .edu.
Take notes in your own words and record the source.
check: Which is often a trusted website ending?
lessons.try: Research a question and take notes from two sources.

learn: A report has an introduction, body paragraphs on subtopics, and a conclusion.
Each body paragraph covers one subtopic, like what bees eat or how they make hives.
List your sources at the end.
check: A report has an introduction, body and...
lessons.try: Turn your research notes into a three-paragraph report.
